subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

textbook_items_in_class.description: Write down the number each child should say (count of taller children ahead) for a given arrangement of seven children of specified heights.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.1 p.128
Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.128
textbook_items_in_class.description: Classify each statement as Always True, Only Sometimes True, or Never True with reasoning: (a) saying '0' means tallest; (b) tallest says '0'; (c) first person says '0'; (d) middle person cannot say '0'; (e) largest number is the shortest; (f) largest possible number in a group of 8.

time_bands.activity: Pose the scenario: seven children stand in a line and each calls out how many taller children are directly in front of them. Students discuss in pairs what information this number sequence captures and what it does not tell us about absolute heights.

Students work through Figure it Out, section 6.1 p.128 ("Write down the number each child should say (count of taller children ahead) for a given arrangement of seven children of specified heights....") — first encoding a given arrangement into a sequence, then attempting to reverse-engineer a valid arrangement from a new sequence, noticing that reconstruction is not always unique.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 6.1 p.128 ("Arrange stick-figure cutouts (or draw) to produce each of these sequences...."), drawing arrangements for several of the given sequences and flagging any sequence that turns out impossible. Class shares findings and discusses why some sequences cannot arise.

Students classify each statement in Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.128 ("Classify each statement as Always True, Only Sometimes True, or Never True with reasoning....") as Always True, Only Sometimes True, or Never True, writing a brief justification. Two or three responses are shared and debated as a class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate 'saying 0' with being the first person in the queue rather than being the tallest person in front of whom no one taller stands — watch for this conflation in Q2(a) and (c). Encourage students to construct a counter-example arrangement whenever they are tempted to mark a statement as Always True.
materials: Squared paper or plain paper for drawing stick-figure arrangements

periods.activity_title: Pair Up, Prove It: Odd and Even Sums

textbook_items_in_class.description: Explore parity of sum of (a) 4 odd numbers; (b) 5 odd numbers; (c) 6 odd numbers using the pair-arrangement model.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the parity of: (a) sum of 2 even + 2 odd numbers; (b) sum of 2 odd + 3 even; (c) sum of 5 even numbers; (d) sum of 8 odd numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Lakpa has odd counts of ₹1 and ₹5 coins and an even count of ₹10 coins; he claims a total of ₹205. Did he make a mistake? Explain why or why not.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.131
homework.description: Determine the parity of: (d) even – even; (e) odd – odd; (f) even – odd; (g) odd – even.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the pair-arrangement picture: draw a small number of dots arranged in pairs to show an even number, then add one extra dot to show an odd number. Ask students to draw pair-pictures for 6, 7, 9, and 12, and to articulate what the leftover dot signals.

Students work through Figure it Out, section 6.2 p.130 ("Explore parity of sum of (a) 4 odd numbers; (b) 5 odd numbers; (c) 6 odd numbers using the pair-arrangement model....") — drawing pair-pictures for each sum and explaining, using the leftover-singles argument, why the total is odd or even. Class builds the generalisation: the parity of a sum of odd numbers depends only on whether the count of odd numbers is itself odd or even.

Students apply the generalisation to Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.131 ("Find the parity of: (a) sum of 2 even + 2 odd numbers....") — deciding parity without computing, and writing a one-sentence justification for each part.

Students reason through Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.131 ("Lakpa has odd counts of ₹1 and ₹5 coins and an even count of ₹10 coins; he claims a total of ₹205....") — determining whether Lakpa's claim is consistent with the parity rules established. Class discusses the parity of ₹205 and what each coin type contributes.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is treating 'sum of odd numbers' as always odd; students need to recognise that pairing the leftover singles from two odd numbers eliminates the remainder. Watch for students who reason from specific examples (3 + 5 = 8) without articulating the general pair argument. Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.131 on subtraction parity is set as a reinforcement task for students to work through independently.
materials: Dot-paper or plain paper for pair-arrangement diagrams

periods.activity_title: Parity in Grids, Coins, and Algebra

textbook_items_in_class.description: Small Squares in Grids: find the parity of the number of squares in (a) 27 × 13 grid; (b) 42 × 78 grid; (c) 135 × 654 grid, without computing the product.

Parity of Expressions: come up with (a) an expression that always has even parity; (b) an expression that always has odd parity; (c) an expression like 3n + 4 that can have either parity. Then determine formulas for the nth even and nth odd number.

time_bands.activity: Warm-up: present the claim that five odd numbers can sum to 30 (Kishor's puzzle from the section). Students write a brief parity argument to accept or refute the claim, then a volunteer explains the reasoning to the class.

Students tackle Figure it Out, section 6.2 p.131 ("Small Squares in Grids: find the parity of the number of squares in (a) 27 × 13 grid; (b) 42 × 78 grid; (c) 135 × 654 grid, without computing the product....") — connecting multiplication parity rules (odd × odd = odd; even × anything = even) to the grid context. Pairs share their reasoning strategy.

Students work through Figure it Out, section 6.2 p.132 ("Parity of Expressions: come up with (a) an expression that always has even parity; (b) an expression that always has odd parity; (c) an expression like 3n + 4 that can have either parity. Then determine formulas for the nth even and nth odd number....") — first proposing their own expressions and testing parity for odd and even values of the variable, then deriving 2n for the nth even number and 2n – 1 for the nth odd number. Selected expressions are shared and scrutinised by the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes write 2n + 1 and 2n – 1 interchangeably for 'all odd numbers' without noticing that the sequence they generate depends on where n starts; ensure students verify their formula against the first three or four terms. The grid problem is a productive bridge between the abstract parity rule for multiplication and a visual context — encourage students who are stuck to test a small grid (3 × 3, 3 × 4) first.

periods.activity_title: Grids, Constraints, and the Magic of 15

textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill two 3 × 3 grids with numbers 1–9 (no repeats) to match the given row and column sums shown in the circles. Also explain why a grid with sums 5 and 26 is impossible.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many different magic squares can be made using numbers 1–9 (ignoring rotations and reflections)?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.3 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Take a magic square and (a) increase each number by 1; (b) double each number. Is the result still a magic square? How do the magic sums change?

time_bands.activity: Students attempt Figure it Out, section 6.3 p.133 ("Fill two 3 × 3 grids with numbers 1–9 (no repeats) to match the given row and column sums shown in the circles. Also explain why a grid with sums 5 and 26 is impossible....") — filling the two target grids and then constructing a written impossibility argument for sums of 5 and 26 using the fact that all nine digits sum to 45.

Class derives the three key properties of the 1–9 magic square: all row/column sums equal 45 ÷ 3 = 15; the centre cell must hold 5 (since every line through the centre sums to 15 and the four lines share only the centre); and 1 and 9 cannot sit in corners. Students record each property as a deductive step, not just an observation.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.136 ("How many different magic squares can be made using numbers 1–9 (ignoring rotations and reflections)?....") — using the established constraints to argue why essentially one arrangement exists, then verify by attempting to place 1 in different non-corner positions.

Students begin Figure it Out Q3, section 6.3 p.136 ("Take a magic square and (a) increase each number by 1; (b) double each number. Is the result still a magic square? How do the magic sums change?....") as a quick investigation — checking whether the magic property is preserved after each operation and recording what happens to the magic sum.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often try to brute-force the grid by guessing rather than using the 45-sum constraint to narrow possibilities; prompt them to compute remaining row sums from what is placed before guessing further entries. The result that essentially only one magic square exists (up to symmetry) is surprising — let students argue it rather than announcing it.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Generalise: if m is the centre of a magic square made from consecutive numbers, express all other entries in terms of m (analogous to the 2 × 2 calendar grid from Chapter 4).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.137
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the generalised form, construct a magic square with centre number 25.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 6.3 p.137
textbook_items_in_class.description: Create a magic square whose magic sum is 60.
Chautīsā Yantra: why is it called 'Chautīsā'? Find other patterns of four numbers in the 4 × 4 square that also add up to 34.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 6.3 p.136
homework.description: Discuss ways of creating a magic square using any set of 9 consecutive numbers (e.g. 2–10, 3–11, 9–17).

time_bands.activity: Using the fact that the centre of a 1–9 magic square is 5 and the magic sum is 15, students work through Math Talk, section 6.3 p.136 ("Generalise: if m is the centre of a magic square made from consecutive numbers, express all other entries in terms of m....") — writing each cell as m plus or minus some offset and verifying that every row, column, and diagonal sums to 3m.

Students apply the generalised form in Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.137 ("Using the generalised form, construct a magic square with centre number 25....") — substituting m = 25 to fill in all cells and checking that each line sums to 75.

Students work through Figure it Out Q4, section 6.3 p.137 ("Create a magic square whose magic sum is 60....") — reasoning that if 3m = 60 then m = 20, substituting into the generalised form, and verifying all line sums.

Students explore Figure it Out, section 6.3 p.137 ("Chautīsā Yantra: why is it called 'Chautīsā'? Find other patterns of four numbers in the 4 × 4 square that also add up to 34....") — reading the historical context of the Khajuraho inscription and identifying at least two patterns of four cells summing to 34.

periods.teacher_notes: The key conceptual leap is writing offsets as ± k from the centre m rather than computing concrete values; students who jump to m = 5 may not see why 3m is the general magic sum. Encourage them to verify the algebra before substituting. The Chautīsā Yantra closing activity works well as a collaborative search — pairs can compare the patterns they find.
materials: Optional: printed image of the Chautīsā Yantra from the textbook page

textbook_segments.title: Nature's Favourite Sequence: The Virahāṅka–Fibonacci Numbers!

periods.activity_title: Building the Virahāṅka Sequence from Rhythms

textbook_items_in_class.description: Write 5 as a sum of 1s and 2s in all possible ways. How many ways are there? Try to find the answer without listing all possibilities. Try for n = 8.
Use the systematic method to write down all 6-beat rhythms (6 as the sum of 1s and 2s in all possible ways). Verify there are 13.
Write the next 3 numbers after 89 in the Virahāṅka sequence. Without computing, determine the parity of the term following 233. Identify the parity pattern of the sequence.

time_bands.activity: Pose the rhythm question: in how many ways can 1 beat, 2 beats, 3 beats, 4 beats be filled with short (1-beat) and long (2-beat) syllables? Students list all possibilities for n = 1, 2, 3, 4 systematically and record the counts in a table.

Students work through Figure it Out, section 6.4 p.140 ("Write 5 as a sum of 1s and 2s in all possible ways. How many ways are there? Try to find the answer without listing all possibilities. Try for n = 8....") — discovering that an n-beat rhythm either starts with a 1-beat syllable (leaving an (n–1)-beat problem) or a 2-beat syllable (leaving an (n–2)-beat problem), and so the count for n equals the sum of the counts for n–1 and n–2.

Students verify the recursive structure for n = 6 in Figure it Out, section 6.4 p.141 ("Use the systematic method to write down all 6-beat rhythms (6 as the sum of 1s and 2s in all possible ways). Verify there are 13....") — listing all rhythms systematically and confirming the count matches the recursion. The sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, … is written out and named.

Students complete Figure it Out, section 6.4 p.142 ("Write the next 3 numbers after 89 in the Virahāṅka sequence. Without computing, determine the parity of the term following 233. Identify the parity pattern of the sequence....") — extending the sequence beyond 89, reading off the parity of the term after 233 using the O-O-E repeating pattern, and articulating why the pattern recurs.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes list rhythms in an unsystematic order and then miscount — encourage a tree structure (branch on first syllable: short or long) to guarantee completeness. The historical note that Virahāṅka (c. 700 CE) named this sequence five centuries before Fibonacci is worth dwelling on briefly; it grounds the naming used throughout this unit and connects to the chapter's theme of mathematics as a living cultural heritage.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Cryptarithms: find what digit each letter stands for in: (a) YY + Z = ZOO; (b) B5 + 3D = ED5; (c) KP + C1 = PRR; (d) KP + C = 1FF.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.5 p.143
textbook_items_in_class.description: A light bulb is ON. Dorjee toggles the switch 77 times. Will the bulb be on or off? Explain using parity.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 6.5 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Solve the cryptarithm: UT + TA = TAT.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 6.5 p.144
homework.description: Make a 3 × 3 magic square with magic sum 0. Not all numbers can be zero; use negative numbers as needed.

time_bands.activity: Walk through the logic of a known worked case: T + T + T = UT gives 3T is a two-digit number ending in T, so T = 5 and U = 1. Establish the two ground rules: each letter stands for a unique digit 0–9, and no leading digit is 0. Students write these rules in their own words.

Students work in pairs through Figure it Out, section 6.5 p.143 ("Cryptarithms: find what digit each letter stands for in: (a) YY + Z = ZOO; (b) B5 + 3D = ED5; (c) KP + C1 = PRR; (d) KP + C = 1FF....") — recording each deductive step explicitly (e.g., 'the units column forces M = …') so their reasoning is visible. Pairs exchange solutions to check.

Students solve Figure it Out Q1, section 6.5 p.143 ("A light bulb is ON. Dorjee toggles the switch 77 times. Will the bulb be on or off? Explain using parity....") — connecting the toggle problem to parity reasoning: 77 is odd, so the final state is the opposite of the initial state.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q11, section 6.5 p.144 ("Solve the cryptarithm: UT + TA = TAT....") — a multi-letter cryptarithm requiring column-by-column deduction and carry reasoning, drawing together the elimination strategies practised throughout this unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often test digits by trial rather than using column constraints to eliminate possibilities systematically; prompt them to start from the units column and ask what carry (0 or 1) is forced before moving to the tens column. Figure it Out Q4, section 6.5 p.144 on a zero-sum magic square using negative numbers is set as a reinforcement task, connecting back to the algebraic magic-square framework built earlier in the chapter.

items.prompt: Four children stand in a line. The sequence of numbers they call out (each saying how many taller children are directly in front of them) is: 0, 0, 1, 2. A classmate says this sequence is impossible. Is the classmate right or wrong? Justify your answer with a brief argument, either constructing a valid arrangement of heights or explaining why no valid arrangement can exist.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The classmate is wrong. The sequence is possible. For example, heights (from front to back) could be: tallest, second-tallest, third (shorter than the second), fourth (shorter than both second and third). Concretely: heights 4, 3, 1, 2 (front to back) give calls 0, 0, 1, 2 — position 3 sees one taller person (height 3) ahead, position 4 sees two taller people (heights 4 and 3) ahead.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reconstruct a height arrangement consistent with the rule that each number equals the count of taller children strictly in front, and verify each position's call matches.

inclusivity.support: Start with just two children to see what calls 0, 0 require, then add a third child to produce the call 1.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a second, different height arrangement that also produces the sequence 0, 0, 1, 2.

exercise.description: Write down the number each child should say (count of taller children ahead) for a given arrangement of seven children of specified heights.

items.prompt: Riya says she added seven odd numbers together and got an even result. Without doing any computation, explain whether Riya's claim can be correct, using the pair-arrangement reasoning about odd and even numbers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Riya's claim cannot be correct. Each odd number, when drawn as a dot arrangement, has one leftover dot after pairing. With seven odd numbers there are seven leftover dots. Seven is itself odd, so those seven extra dots cannot all be paired up — one remains unpaired. The total therefore has an unpaired dot, making it odd, not even.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the pair-arrangement argument: the number of leftover singles equals the count of odd addends; since 7 is odd, the total is odd.

inclusivity.support: Draw pair-pictures for two small odd numbers (e.g. 3 and 5) and count the leftover dots before reasoning about seven numbers.
inclusivity.challenge: State a general rule: the sum of n odd numbers is odd if and only if n is odd, and prove it using the leftover-singles argument for any n.

exercise.description: Explore parity of sum of (a) 4 odd numbers; (b) 5 odd numbers; (c) 6 odd numbers using the pair-arrangement model.

items.prompt: A student claims she can fill a 3 × 3 grid with the digits 1 through 9 (each used exactly once) so that every row sum and every column sum equals 16. Using the properties of the digit sum 1 + 2 + … + 9 = 45, explain why this is impossible. Then state, with justification, the one value that all row sums (and all column sums) must share in any such grid.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: If every row sum were 16, the total of all three row sums would be 3 × 16 = 48. But the total of all nine digits 1 through 9 is 45, so the three row sums must add to 45, not 48. The claim therefore leads to a contradiction and is impossible. For any valid grid using 1–9 exactly once, the three row sums must add to 45, so each row sum equals 45 ÷ 3 = 15. The same argument applies to columns.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The sum of all nine entries equals 45; dividing by 3 (the number of rows or columns) forces each row/column sum to be exactly 15.

inclusivity.support: First compute 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 9 together as a class, then ask what three equal shares of this total would each be.
inclusivity.challenge: Extend the argument: if the digits used were 2 through 10 instead of 1 through 9, what would the forced row sum be, and why?

exercise.description: Fill two 3 × 3 grids with numbers 1–9 (no repeats) to match the given row and column sums shown in the circles. Also explain why a grid with sums 5 and 26 is impossible.

items.section_title: Nature's Favourite Sequence: The Virahāṅka–Fibonacci Numbers!
items.prompt: The number of ways to fill an n-beat rhythm with short (1-beat) and long (2-beat) syllables follows the Virahāṅka sequence. Explain, using the argument about what the first syllable of an n-beat rhythm must be, why the count for n beats always equals the sum of the counts for (n – 1) beats and (n – 2) beats.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any n-beat rhythm must begin with either a short (1-beat) or a long (2-beat) syllable. If it begins with a short syllable, the remaining beats form an (n – 1)-beat rhythm, and there are as many such continuations as there are (n – 1)-beat rhythms. If it begins with a long syllable, the remaining beats form an (n – 2)-beat rhythm, giving as many continuations as (n – 2)-beat rhythms. Since these two cases are exhaustive and mutually exclusive, the total count for n beats is the count for (n – 1) beats plus the count for (n – 2) beats.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Partition all n-beat rhythms by their first syllable (short or long) to show the two cases are disjoint and exhaustive, each reducing to a smaller sub-problem.

inclusivity.support: List all rhythms for n = 3 and n = 4 first, then ask a partner to match each 4-beat rhythm to one that starts with a short syllable or one that starts with a long syllable.
inclusivity.challenge: Alter the premise: suppose syllables could be 1-beat, 2-beat, or 3-beat. Derive the analogous recurrence for the count of n-beat rhythms in this new setting.

exercise.description: Write 5 as a sum of 1s and 2s in all possible ways. How many ways are there? Try to find the answer without listing all possibilities. Try for n = 8.

items.prompt: A rectangular grid has 45 rows and 28 columns. Without multiplying, what is the parity of the total number of small squares in the grid?

options.label: A
options.text: Even, because one of the two dimensions is even.

options.label: B
options.text: Odd, because 45 is odd and determines the parity of the product.

options.label: C
options.text: Even, because both dimensions are greater than 1.

options.label: D
options.text: Odd, because the sum 45 + 28 = 73 is odd.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Even. The total number of squares equals 45 × 28. Since 28 is even, the product is even regardless of 45, because any integer multiplied by an even number is even.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the parity rule for multiplication: even × anything = even; since 28 is even, 45 × 28 is even.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student believes only the odd factor determines the product's parity, not recognising that an even factor forces an even product.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has invented a false rule connecting size of factors to parity, rather than using the odd/even multiplication rule.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is confusing the parity of a sum of two numbers with the parity of their product.

inclusivity.support: Test with a small case first: what is the parity of 3 × 4? Use a dot-grid picture to see why an even number of columns always gives an even total.
inclusivity.challenge: Change 28 to 29 and re-decide the parity; then state a general rule for when a product of two integers is odd.

exercise.description: Small Squares in Grids: find the parity of the number of squares in (a) 27 × 13 grid; (b) 42 × 78 grid; (c) 135 × 654 grid, without computing the product.

items.prompt: The centre of a 3 × 3 magic square made from nine consecutive integers is 11. Using the generalised form in which every entry is expressed as m plus or minus a fixed offset (where m is the centre), write down the complete magic square and verify that one row, one column, and one diagonal each sum to 3m. State the value of the magic sum.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: With m = 11, the nine consecutive integers are 7 through 15 with centre 11. The standard generalised arrangement (using offsets ±1, ±2, ±3, ±4) places the entries as: top row: m–1, m+4, m–3 = 10, 15, 8; middle row: m–4, m, m+4 — wait, the standard 1–9 magic square scaled to centre m gives: top-left = m–1 = 10, top-centre = m+4 = 15, top-right = m–3 = 8; mid-left = m–4 = 7, mid-centre = m = 11, mid-right = m+4 — The standard offsets for the unique 3×3 magic square (mapped from 1–9 with centre 5) are: positions relative to centre: top-left = m–1, top-mid = m+4 = 15, top-right = m–3; left = m–4 = 7, centre = m = 11, right = m+4 = 15 — to avoid conflict use the canonical offset set: {−4, −3, −2, −1, 0, +1, +2, +3, +4}. Canonical arrangement: top row 10, 15, 8; middle row 7, 11, 15 — digits must all differ; the correct unique magic square with centre 11 is: top row: m–1=10, m+4=15, m–3=8 → sum 33 = 3×11 ✓; middle row: m–4=7, m=11, m+4 is already 15 — conflict. Correct canonical offsets from the 1–9 square (where 5 is centre): entries are 2,7,6 / 9,5,1 / 4,3,8; subtract 5, offsets are −3,+2,+1 / +4,0,−4 / −1,−2,+3. With m=11: top row 8,13,12; middle row 15,11,7; bottom row 10,9,14. Check top row: 8+13+12=33=3×11 ✓; middle row: 15+11+7=33 ✓; bottom row: 10+9+14=33 ✓; left column: 8+15+10=33 ✓; main diagonal: 8+11+14=33 ✓. Magic sum = 33.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Derive offsets from the standard 1–9 magic square by subtracting 5 (its centre), then add m = 11 to each offset to build the new square; verify rows, columns, and diagonals sum to 3m = 33.

inclusivity.support: Start by writing out the known 1–9 magic square, then subtract 5 from every entry to see the offset pattern before substituting m = 11.
inclusivity.challenge: Verify that the anti-diagonal (top-right to bottom-left) also sums to 33, then explain algebraically using the offsets why both diagonals must equal 3m.

exercise.description: Generalise: if m is the centre of a magic square made from consecutive numbers, express all other entries in terms of m (analogous to the 2 × 2 calendar grid from Chapter 4).

items.prompt: In the cryptarithm AB + BA = CDC, each letter stands for a different digit (0–9), no leading digit is 0, and A ≠ B. Find the digits A, B, C, and D. Show each deductive step.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: AB + BA means (10A + B) + (10B + A) = 11A + 11B = 11(A + B). So CDC = 11(A + B). CDC is a three-digit palindrome of the form 100C + 10D + C = 101C + 10D. We need 11(A + B) to be a three-digit palindrome. Since A and B are single non-zero digits (A ≠ 0, B ≠ 0) and A ≠ B, A + B ranges from 3 to 17. 11 × (A + B) must be three digits: A + B ≥ 10 gives 110, 121, 132, …, 187. Check which are palindromes of form CDC: 121 = 11×11 → C=1, D=2, A+B=11. 11×12=132 (not palindrome). 11×13=143 (not palindrome). 11×14=154 (not palindrome). 11×15=165 (not palindrome). 11×16=176 (not palindrome). 11×17=187 (not palindrome). Only 121 works: C=1, D=2, A+B=11. Choose A=4, B=7 (or any pair summing to 11 with A≠B, neither 0, and all four letters distinct). With A=4, B=7: 47+74=121 ✓. C=1, D=2 are distinct from A=4 and B=7. Valid solution: A=4, B=7, C=1, D=2 (or equivalently A=7, B=4).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Express AB + BA = 11(A+B), identify which multiples of 11 in the three-digit range are palindromes of form CDC, then choose valid digit pairs summing to the required value.

inclusivity.support: Expand AB and BA in place-value form (tens and units) and add them to see that the sum equals 11 times something before searching for the palindrome.
inclusivity.challenge: Determine all valid (A, B) pairs for the solution found, and explain why no other multiple of 11 can produce a CDC palindrome.

exercise.description: Cryptarithms: find what digit each letter stands for in: (a) YY + Z = ZOO; (b) B5 + 3D = ED5; (c) KP + C1 = PRR; (d) KP + C = 1FF.
